events.title: Jan Hus burned at Constance
events.shortBlurb: The Bohemian preacher was condemned by the Council of Constance and burned at the stake…
body: Born at Husinec in southern Bohemia about 1369, Jan Hus took his master's degree at the University of Prague, was ordained priest in 1400, and served as rector of the university and preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel, where his Czech sermons drew great crowds.

Formed by the writings of John Wyclif, he attacked the clergy's morals and challenged received teaching on the Church and the papacy; excommunicated in 1410 and again in 1411, he left Prague and wrote his chief work, De ecclesia. Given a safe-conduct by King Sigismund, he went to the Council of Constance in November 1414, only to be imprisoned within weeks and tried for heresy.

Refusing to recant propositions he disowned, he was degraded from the priesthood and handed to the secular arm, and on 6 July 1415 was burned outside the city, his ashes thrown into the Rhine. Jerome of Prague followed him to the stake in 1416. Bohemia answered his death with defiance, and the Hussite Wars that broke out in 1419 ravaged the kingdom for some fifteen years.

events.title: The execution of St. Thomas More
events.shortBlurb: England's former Lord Chancellor died on the scaffold rather than deny the authority of the Church…
body: Born in London in 1478, Thomas More rose from the bar to the House of Commons, made his name across Europe with Utopia in 1516, and in October 1529 succeeded Cardinal Wolsey as Lord Chancellor, the first layman to hold that office. Unable to approve the king's divorce or his claim over the Church, he resigned in May 1532.

When the Act of Succession required an oath repudiating the pope's authority, More refused it at Lambeth on 14 April 1534 and was committed to the Tower. After fifteen months he was tried for treason at Westminster Hall on 1 July 1535 and convicted chiefly on the word of Richard Rich, whom he openly branded a perjurer.

Sentenced to be hanged at Tyburn, he was spared that shame by the king and beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535, declaring that he died "the King's good servant, but God's first." Beatified by Leo XIII in 1886 and canonized with John Fisher by Pius XI in 1935, he was proclaimed patron of statesmen and politicians by John Paul II in 2000.
